_comment: Each fixture is a real RCSB entry chosen because probe_entry.py MEASURED the shape in
the downloaded file. 'evidence' is what that tool reported -- not a claim from the
literature and not a recollection. Re-run tests/probe_entry.py against the download
directory to confirm the entries still carry these shapes.
'expect' entries with "status": "open" are known, documented gaps: check_fixtures.py
reports them as GAP and does not fail the run. Fixing one means deleting its status
field, at which point the suite enforces it.

fixtures.shape: Fab with Kabat insertion codes in CDR-H2 and CDR-H3
fixtures.evidence: 4 chains; 3 distinct insertion codes (A,B,C); 6 author numbers covering more than one residue; 80 zero-occupancy atoms
fixtures.why: Chain H carries 52A (CDR-H2), 82A/B/C (FR3) and 100A/B/C (CDR-H3). The CDR residues are exactly the ones a user would name as hotspots on an antibody target.

fixtures.shape: intact IgG: insertion codes plus N-linked glycans
fixtures.evidence: 4 chains; 7 insertion codes; 6 duplicate author numbers; 6 non-polymer components (BMA,FUC,FUL,GAL,MAN,NAG); 18 zero-occupancy atoms
fixtures.why: Same insertion-code shape as 12E8 but with branched glycans attached, so it also exercises the non-polymer path.

fixtures.evidence: 20 models in pdbx_PDB_model_num; 1 chain; 41620 atom rows
fixtures.why: Smallest honest multi-model case: 2081 atoms present 20 times over.

fixtures.evidence: 640 models; 1 chain; 787840 atom rows for a 76-residue protein
fixtures.why: The size at which passing an ensemble through is unmissable: 640 superimposed copies of the target would reach RFD4 as one structure.

fixtures.shape: zinc finger: NMR ensemble, bound Zn, capped termini
fixtures.evidence: 37 models; 1 ZN non-polymer; 2 modified polymer components (ACE,NH2); 333 HETATM carrying a label_seq_id
fixtures.why: Three shapes at once, and the Zn is structural -- deleting it silently changes what the target is.

fixtures.shape: haemoglobin: 4 chains, haem cofactor, A/B altlocs
fixtures.evidence: 4 chains; 1 HEM non-polymer; altlocs A,B; 37 zero-occupancy atoms
fixtures.why: The haem sits at the chain interface, so dropping it changes the interface the design is scored against.

fixtures.shape: barnase-barstar, 6 chains (three copies of the complex)
fixtures.evidence: 6 chains; altlocs A,B; no insertion codes
fixtures.why: Five of six chains are dropped by the contig. A user who picked this entry for its interface should be told which copy survived.

fixtures.shape: macrocyclic peptide bound to PD-L1 (this workflow's own sample input)
fixtures.evidence: 2 chains; 5 modified polymer components (9KK,CCS,MEA,NH2,SAR); 106 HETATM carrying a label_seq_id; 44 zero-occupancy atoms; altlocs A,B,C
fixtures.why: The entry that first showed HETATM filtering shortens a chain. Also the only fixture with an altloc beyond B.

fixtures.shape: the same macrocycle entry, taken through the PDB conversion path
fixtures.evidence: chain B is 15 residues, 7 non-standard (MEA, 9KK, SAR, MEA, SAR, CCS, NH2); 14 carry a full N/CA/C backbone and NH2 is an amide cap carrying only N; the chain's waters start at 101
fixtures.why: A PDB file has no label_seq_id, so node 01 assigns it. Deciding polymer membership from the ATOM/HETATM flag deleted every modified residue: this chain came out as 8 residues reporting n_nonstandard=0, which also disarmed the warning that exists to catch a heavily modified chain. The same entry as the mmCIF fixture above, so the two paths can be compared directly.

fixtures.evidence: 1 model; 1 chain; no insertion codes, no modified residues, no non-polymer, no altlocs, no zero-occupancy atoms
fixtures.why: Control. Any failure here is the harness or a regression in the common path, not an exotic input.

fixtures.evidence: 2 chains; 1 NA ion; no insertion codes, no modified residues, no altlocs
fixtures.why: The example the README is written around. If this stops working the documentation is wrong.

_rejections_comment: Inputs node 02 must REFUSE, and one it must still accept. A guard that cannot be shown refusing is not a guard.

rejections.name: target-first contig is refused
rejections.why: RFD4 writes chains in contig order and node 04 reads the first chain as the design, so a contig naming the target first makes designed_chain, designed_length, the designed sequence, the hydrophobic fraction, the net charge and the radius of gyration all describe the target. Nothing downstream can notice: the chain count is unchanged and every number is plausible.

rejections.name: designed-first contig is still accepted
rejections.why: The guard above must not cost a legitimate override.

_node04_comment: Node 03 needs a GPU and minutes per design, so node 04 is tested on structures built by tests/make_designs.py. Node 04 reads only chain ids, residue names, sequence numbers and CA coordinates, so a hand-built two-chain mmCIF exercises it exactly as a real design does -- and deterministically, which a sampled design never could.

node04.name: designed-chain-is-first
node04.why: Pins the convention node 02's contig guard exists to protect.

node04.name: reversed-chain-order
node04.why: The same atoms with the chains written in the opposite order. Node 04 still cannot tell, which is why the guard lives in node 02; this keeps the residual gap visible rather than remembered.

node04.name: ordering-at-12-designs
node04.why: Lexicographic sort puts design_10 and design_11 between design_1 and design_2. Display order only -- every row carries its own name, and nodes 05 and 06 key by name rather than by position -- but a reader reconciling the table against a run directory should not have to work that out.
